name: Pasteurisation of wine in France
summary: Louis Pasteur showed at Arbois that microbes spoil wine and in 1865 patented gentle heating to kill them, the process later used for beer and milk.
description: Louis Pasteur, working from the vineyards of Arbois, showed that the diseases of wine were caused by microbes and in 1865 patented a process of heating wine to between 60 and 100 degrees Celsius to kill them. The process came to be called pasteurization and was later applied to beer, milk and other foods.

impact.note: Heat treatment descended from this work is now applied to milk, beer, juice and other foods eaten by most people in most regions; it made milk and bottled drinks safe to store and ship and reorganised dairying around it, with a few direct successors such as later milk processes.

why: French wine exported to Britain was arriving undrinkable, and the economic stakes were high enough that Napoleon III asked Pasteur in 1863 to find the causes of the wine diseases and a way to prevent them.

date.label: 11 April 1865
date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

events.statement: Louis Pasteur filed a patent on 11 April 1865 for a process of preserving wine by killing the microbes in it, for which heating the wine to between 60 and 100 degrees Celsius was the method given.

evidence.supports: On April 11, 1865, Pasteur filed a patient "for a process for the preservation of wine": "Wine does not spoil if the microbes are killed beforehand. A simple, practical method is to heat the wine to a temperature between 60 and 100°C."
evidence.locator: Section: Pasteurization, an invention to save wine

earliest_record.rationale: The earliest dated evidence found for this capability in this community. No review has yet confirmed that nothing earlier exists.

unresolved.note: Whether Pasteur drew on Appert's heat preservation (already in the dataset as appert-sealed-food-preservation) or on earlier heated-wine practice is unresolved; the lead mentions Japanese sake heating in the sixteenth century, which was not verified here.
The Institut Pasteur dates the recommendation to use the process on milk to 1866, by a German chemist; the lead gives the 1880s. Not resolved.
The place where the patent was filed is not given by the source; Arbois is where the source places the work on wine.
Pasteur's years of birth and death are not on the page read and are left empty.

research.note: The Institut Pasteur says the principle of heating had been known for some time before the 1865 patent; the sources read do not say whether Pasteur drew on earlier heat preservation, so independence is not settled.
